title: Ensemble learning for day-ahead district heat load forecasting: Base learners, ensemble structures, and combination rules across training data partitioning strategies
abstract: Data-driven models can achieve high accuracy in district heat load forecasting, yet no single model performs best across tasks and systems, motivating ensemble learning based on diverse base learners. Studies predominantly evaluate fixed ensemble configurations, leaving component contributions unquantified and informed training data partitioning uncontrolled against random partitioning. To quantify these contributions to day-ahead district heat load forecasting, we deconstruct ensemble models into base learner algorithm, ensemble structure, and combination rule, comparing four regression algorithms, homogeneous and heterogeneous structures, and three dynamic combination rules across five training data partitioning strategies, including a random control and a temperature-based seasonal rule. All configurations are benchmarked prequentially on a controlled synthetic and an operational real-world dataset. Homogeneous ensembles of non-linear algorithms under random partitioning with dynamic error-based weighting reduce MAE by 7.3 % on synthetic data and 15.7 % on real-world data over the respective single models, with improvements persisting across partition realizations. On both datasets, the heterogeneous ensemble trained on the complete dataset remains within the statistically best model group, indicating a favorable default configuration. Linear regression benefits most, reducing MAE by up to 52.4 % through informed partitioning and dynamic selection, narrowly outperforming the best single model on real-world data. Performance is governed not by the cohesion and separation of load profiles across partitions but by the balance between specialization and available training data, rendering the value of partitioning algorithm-specific. The findings yield practical recommendations for batch-based ensemble model initialization and combination rule selection ahead of data stream deployment.

title: What the survey literature says about reinforcement learning for building control: A critical synthesis
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has attracted growing interest for building control and optimization, as reflected in 22 survey papers. Yet their insights remain fragmented. We therefore conduct a tertiary review of these surveys. Across seven research questions, we examine algorithm characterization, control formulation and comparability, subsystem coverage, occupant modeling, validation and sim-to-real transfer, reproducibility, and changing research priorities. Three systemic patterns emerge in how the reviews represent the field. First, a comparability gap persists: surveys describe states, actions, rewards, and constraints sufficiently to communicate the general RL framing, but not consistently enough to support cross-study comparison. Second, a subsystem and occupant concentration is evident: HVAC and thermal comfort dominate, whereas indoor air quality, lighting, electric-vehicle coupling, district-scale coordination, and personalization remain underdeveloped review topics. Third, a deployment evidence gap remains: simulation is the dominant validation setting, and field evidence, which appears in the most recent reviews, remains concentrated in few installations and difficult to compare. Emphasis also varies across the corpus, from algorithm-centered characterizationtoward multi-agent coordination, safety- and constraint-aware control, and standardized benchmarking; this reflects variation among the reviews rather than a measured trend. Overall, the survey literature treats feasibility in simulation as established and identifies integration, safety, reproducibility, and deployment as the more persistent challenges. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first cross-survey synthesis of RL for building control. It clarifies where surveys converge and diverge and directs future research toward more comparable, deployable, and trustworthy RL-based building control.

title: From predictive accuracy to decision reliability in the scarce data regime: A surrogate–calibration framework for battery thermal management optimisation
abstract: Thermal management is critical to battery safety, durability, and performance, but multi-objective battery thermal management system design commonly relies on computationally expensive high-fidelity simulations. Surrogate models can reduce this cost, yet in the scarce-data regime a surrogate with acceptable point-prediction accuracy may still provide miscalibrated predictive uncertainty. This becomes important when uncertainty is used directly to guide Pareto search, because overconfident predictions can make weakly supported designs appear artificially attractive. This work develops a surrogate–calibration framework for fixed-data battery thermal management optimisation. Gaussian-process-based surrogates are selected using validation performance and stabilised through bagging. Their model-based predictive uncertainty is then empirically rescaled using cross-fitted conformal scale calibration. The evaluation is organised across three complementary levels that introduce different physical and numerical challenges. Analytical benchmarks provide controlled ground truth while varying input dimensionality and Pareto-front geometry. Two public battery thermal management datasets introduce different cooling configurations, objective structures, and realistic scarce-data conditions. An in-house computational fluid dynamics case provides the most direct decision-level test by combining a structured four-dimensional dataset with continuous off-grid thermo-hydraulic optimisation and independent high-fidelity verification of selected designs. The results support empirical uncertainty calibration as a practical safeguard for surrogate-assisted battery thermal management design under data scarcity, while also highlighting the importance of direct high-fidelity verification in sparsely supported regions.

title: Application of reinforcement learning for multigroup energy grid optimization for neutron transport criticality problems
abstract: The optimization of energy group structures is integral to the accuracy of multigroup neutron transport calculations. This work introduces the use of reinforcement learning (RL) with surrogate modeling to optimize group structures for one-dimensional spherical 𝑘 -eigenvalue problems. The proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm is adapted to energy grid structures, with a reward based on the predicted accuracy of each intermediate structure and a terminal reward for accurate final structures. Starting from a high-fidelity energy grid, the agent removes energy bounds until a target number of groups is reached, with all candidate structures restricted to subsets of the LANL618 group structure. The agent is trained to maximize the return over an entire episode rather than the immediate error, accepting intermediate removals that lead to more accurate final structures. Neural network surrogate models that incorporate energy, material, and spatial information replace transport simulations during RL training. Applied to the Godiva and BeRP ball problems, the RL-constructed 30 group structures have lower errors than LANL30, and the 70 group structures match or improve on LANL70. The RL model outperforms or is comparable to previous optimization methods including hierarchical agglomeration, particle swarm optimization, a genetic algorithm, and simulated annealing. Within each problem family, the trained policy can be reused for new starting group structures and material layouts without additional transport simulations, demonstrating the flexibility of the RL approach.

title: Optimal structural design of electric submersible pumps based on deep learning and the NSGA-II method
abstract: Existing electrical submersible pumps face challenges including low efficiency, narrow operating ranges, and difficulties in synergetic multi-objective optimization. To address these issues, this study proposes a multi-objective optimization framework integrating computational fluid dynamics, deep learning surrogate models, and the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) for the structural optimization of a mixed-flow pump. Parametric modeling and constraint formulation are conducted for 15 critical geometric variables. Based on the defined design space, an initial dataset is generated via optimal Latin hypercube sampling, with each sample evaluated using high-fidelity simulations. Key parameters significantly influencing head and efficiency are analyzed through the Plackett–Burman method. Subsequently, a deep learning model is developed to characterize the nonlinear mapping between structural parameters and hydraulic performance. The NSGA-II algorithm is applied to explore the Pareto-optimal solutions, enabling effective multi-objective synergy between head and efficiency. The findings demonstrate that single-point optimization at the target flow rate improves hydraulic performance throughout the investigated flow-rate range and widens the high-efficiency range. The optimized design also reduces hydraulic losses and enhances impeller–diffuser matching. Compared with the baseline mixed-flow pump, the optimized structure achieves an 16.82% higher head and a 27.20% increase in the peak efficiency. This methodology effectively balances output and efficiency while enhancing wide-range operational adaptability, offering a systematic and reliable approach for electrical submersible pump design and optimization.

title: Time-series foundation models for energy infrastructure: Evidence and requirements for digital-twin-grade integration
abstract: Time-series foundation models promise reusable forecasting across heterogeneous energy systems, but their readiness for operational digital twins remains unclear. This structured critical review evaluates that gap through a documented literature search and targeted follow-up completed on 28 September 2026. Five initial web queries and three subsequently added queries returned 164 records; screening and targeted follow-up yielded a core evidence corpus of 42 studies, complemented by selectively sampled contextual literature on operational requirements. Study-level extraction distinguishes direct energy evidence, transferred enabling evidence and proposed integration functions, while a qualitative maturity assessment links each judgement to supporting studies and limitations. The evidence shows conditional forecasting benefits rather than universal superiority: a district-heating study reports annual normalized errors of 12.48% for a pretrained model and 14.57% for a task-specific transformer under observed future weather, whereas an electricity-price benchmark finds no foundation model statistically superior to its seasonal decomposition baseline overall. Recent studies also demonstrate building classification, graph-conditioned prediction and physics-informed adaptation. However, the strongest evidence remains retrospective and forecasting-focused; reliable fault isolation, maintenance benefit and controlled prospective operational improvement are not yet established. To translate these gaps into an actionable evaluation framework, a worked district-heating workflow specifies forecast-origin information, local calibration, physical simulation, abstention and prospective consequence assessment. Digital-twin-grade integration is therefore framed as a system-level assessment requiring locally verified uncertainty, leakage-aware evaluation and governed operation, rather than as an intrinsic property of a pretrained checkpoint.

title: From nodes to edges: Edge-centric GNNs for distribution grid reliability
abstract: Edge classification remains challenging for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), as most standard architectures are designed primarily for node- or graph-level prediction. In many applications, however, decisions depend on identifying critical edges rather than individual nodes or entire graphs. This paper studies edge classification on graph-structured data and introduces GINEE (GIN with Evolving Edges), an edge-centric GNN that explicitly maintains and updates edge representations across message-passing layers using an update rule that is invariant to the labelling of an edge’s two endpoints, together with a controlled ablation that separately quantifies the contribution of edge features, evolving edge states, and node–edge co-evolution. We focus on medium-voltage power grids as a safety-critical application domain, where edge classification corresponds to identifying cables whose outage leads to a violation of the n-1 contingency criterion. In this setting, we show that a node-centric baseline (GIN) achieves low recall on critical edges compared to edge-aware formulations. We evaluate GINEE against GIN variants with static edge embeddings and a line-graph-based formulation that enables direct edge–edge message passing. Experiments on realistic medium-voltage grid data from a Dutch DSO show that GINEE achieves the best overall recall and balanced accuracy: explicit edge features account for most of the performance gain, while evolving edge states provide a further consistent improvement. The line-graph reformulation underperforms edge-aware models on the original graph and incurs substantially higher inference cost, suggesting that explicit edge modelling without graph transformation is the more effective inductive bias for safety-critical edge classification.

title: DARLIN: Domain-guided augmented retrieval for LLM-based interpretable and transferable HVAC control
abstract: Advanced HVAC control strategies such as Model Predictive Control and Reinforcement Learning can deliver substantial energy savings but face persistent barriers to adoption, including reliance on building-specific models or extensive training datasets, limited transferability across buildings and climates, and opaque decision-making. We introduce DARLIN, a retrieval-augmented framework that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to control HVAC cooling setpoints. At each control step, DARLIN retrieves guidance from a knowledge base built from thousands of building science papers, combines it with real-time system observations, and generates a short-horizon cooling setpoint trajectory together with a human-readable rationale. In a calibrated EnergyPlus simulation of an office building, DARLIN reduced cooling energy by 7.6% relative to a rule-based control baseline in a mild climate, while improving occupant comfort, which the baseline degraded through afternoon overcooling. Analysis of generated rationales shows trend-aware, anticipatory, history-informed, and corrective reasoning, with each setpoint decision traceable to a stated condition and a cited strategy. Applied to a different building across 15 climates with no building- and climate-specific changes, DARLIN achieved an average cooling energy saving of 17.7% and improved comfort in 11 of the 15 climates; in the four cities with humid tropical and subtropical climates, however, its temperature-focused prompt failed to maintain comfort, as raising the setpoint to save energy impaired latent-heat removal and shifted discomfort to the warm side. A controlled ablation that removes the retrieved domain knowledge confirms that the RAG-based domain guidance, rather than the LLM’s zero-shot reasoning, drives these energy and comfort gains, and a repeated-inference study together with a deterministic output-validation and safety layer shows that DARLIN operates reliably with a stochastic LLM, keeping every applied action valid and bounded. By combining LLM reasoning with domain knowledge, DARLIN offers a scalable, transferable, and interpretable approach to intelligent building control and energy utilization.

title: Tail reliability of machine-learning probabilistic forecasts in the GB day-ahead electricity market
abstract: Probabilistic forecasts of day-ahead electricity prices are increasingly used to manage price risk, yet competing models are usually ranked on aggregate scores that average over the price regimes in which uncertainty matters most. This study evaluates probabilistic forecasts of hourly EPEX SPOT GB day-ahead prices over a full out-of-sample calendar year, applying a common pre-auction information boundary and prequential rolling-origin design to linear quantile regression, a quantile regression forest (QRF), a LEAR-QRA benchmark and an encoder-decoder quantile long short-term memory (LSTM) network. Two routes to more reliable intervals are then compared: conformal recalibration and Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA). Aggregate scores separate the LSTM and QRF only weakly, with a non-significant 4.4% difference in continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), but their conditional behaviour differs sharply. Above 200 GBP/MWh the LSTM covered 0.12 of outcomes and QRF 0.71, a difference of 0.60 whose 95% bootstrap interval excludes zero under both day- and episode-level resampling. Conformal recalibration corrected marginal coverage but did not improve the interval score or materially repair spike coverage. QRA combining the LSTM, QRF and LEAR-QRA forecasts reduced CRPS to 5.14 GBP/MWh and raised coverage above 200 GBP/MWh to 0.65 at essentially unchanged interval width. Pooled conformal recalibration and combination therefore address different failures and are not substitutes.

title: Model predictive-fractional control with support vector machine-based FDI detection for smart grid frequency regulation
abstract: The increasing integration of renewable energy sources and communication infrastructures has transformed conventional power systems into cyber–physical smart grids, increasing their exposure to cyberattacks. False Data Injection (FDI) attacks are particularly challenging for load frequency control (LFC) because manipulated feedback measurements can degrade frequency regulation and inter-area power exchange. This paper proposes a cyber–resilient LFC framework for a three-area renewable-integrated smart grid combining attack detection, supervisory mitigation, and optimized frequency control. An Anomaly Identification Framework based on a Support Vector Machine optimized through Grid Search (SVM–GS) is developed using point-wise system measurements, while an Arctic Puffin Optimization (APO)-tuned hybrid model predictive–fractional controller regulates frequency and tie-line power under operational disturbances and cyber threats. Upon attack detection, the compromised measurement is isolated and replaced with a buffered trusted pre-attack reference while retaining the same controller structure. Simulation results demonstrate that, under trajectory-wise evaluation, the proposed SVM–GS detector achieves an accuracy of 99.9963%, a precision of 99.9950%, a recall of 99.9975%, and an F 1 -score of 99.9963% on completely held-out simulation scenarios. In the closed-loop cyber-resilience assessment, the two imposed FDI events were detected after 6.28 s and 4.66 s, respectively. Under normal load disturbances, the maximum frequency deviations were limited to 0.0910– 0 . 0 9 2 0 × 1 ⁢ 0 − 4 Hz and the maximum tie-line deviations to 0.027– 0 . 0 3 8 × 1 ⁢ 0 − 5 pu MW across the three areas. These results demonstrate that coordinated machine-learning-based detection, measurement protection, and advanced control can enhance the resilience of renewable-integrated smart-grid frequency regulation.
